decisions.mark: locates the macro's definition in include/mbedtls/private_access.h
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `include/mbedtls/private_access.h` makes `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member)` expand to `private_##member` by default, and to plain `member` only when `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined. | WHY: The answer explicitly says the macro is defined in include/mbedtls/private_access.h and describes its expansion.

decisions.mark: states that by default the macro RENAMES the member to private_<member>, and that defining MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS makes it expand to the member name unchanged
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member)` expand to `private_##member` by default, and to plain `member` only when `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined. | WHY: The answer explicitly states both the default renaming to private_<member> and the unchanged expansion when MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS is defined.

decisions.mark: explains that the two branches give different consumers different views — code that defines MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS sees plain member names while an ordinary consumer of the public headers sees the renamed ones
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(member)` expand to `private_##member` by default, and to plain `member` only when `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` is defined. | WHY: The answer states that code defining the macro sees plain member names while the default consumer sees `private_`-renamed ones, and it covers who gets each view.

decisions.mark: concludes that this enforces API opacity at COMPILE time by breaking the member name, rather than by hiding the struct layout — the fields remain visible and sized
decisions.detail: QUOTE: This is a source-level gate, not encapsulation. The struct layout stays in the public header, so `sizeof` and offsets are still visible. What the macro buys is that accidental or unsupported field access fails to compile | WHY: The answer says opacity is enforced at compile time by renaming the member to `private_<name>`, while the layout and sizes stay visible.

decisions.mark: conveys that the macro is applied at a scale of many hundreds of sites, overwhelmingly in the public headers rather than in library implementation
decisions.detail: QUOTE: "include/mbedtls/ssl.h` has 209 uses" and "Public structs use it throughout" | WHY: The answer gives a count only for ssl.h (209) and says "throughout" public structs, but it never conveys a scale of many hundreds of sites overall, nor that the uses are overwhelmingly in public headers rather than library implementation. It actually says only three library files use the macro directly, which is a different claim.

decisions.mark: states that library-internal code turns the opt-out ON in a shared header, so every library translation unit sees plain member names
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `library/common.h:132` defines `MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS` unconditionally... `library/common.h` is internal and not installed, and 107 library `.c` files include it. Inside those files, `MBEDTLS_PRIVATE(x)` resolves to the real `x`. | WHY: The answer states that library-internal code enables the opt-out in the shared header `library/common.h`, so library translation units see plain member names.

decisions.mark: identifies that some example programs ALSO define the opt-out for themselves, deliberately reaching past the public API they otherwise demonstrate
decisions.detail: QUOTE: `programs/ssl/ssl_client2.c:8` and `programs/ssl/ssl_server2.c:8` define the macro as their first line, before any include. They use it to inspect internal SSL state | WHY: The answer states that example programs (ssl_client2, ssl_server2) define MBEDTLS_ALLOW_PRIVATE_ACCESS themselves, bypassing the gate.
